title: The One With The Birth

jokes.text: Ross panicking that Carol isn't at the hospital yet while she's in labor
jokes.setup: Ross is frantic that Carol isn't at the hospital for the birth of his child
jokes.punchline: She's not here yet. She's having my baby and she's not here.
jokes.explanation: Functional character comedy — Ross's neurotic panic is on-brand, but the joke is basically just setup for the episode's premise. Mild chuckle at best.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: The placenta was still attached and—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Ross! We don't need the play-by-play!

jokes.text: But when I spoke to her, she said she'd already passed the mucus plug. [GROANS from group]
jokes.setup: The group asks whether Carol's water has broken as a measure of how far along she is.
jokes.punchline: Ross overshares clinical birth detail (mucus plug), causing collective groaning disgust from everyone present.
jokes.explanation: The groan reaction sells it. Ross's clinical oversharing is a reliable character beat, and 'mucus plug' is inherently unpleasant enough to generate a visceral audience reaction. The group's synchronized disgust is the actual punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: When I have a kid, I'm gonna be one of those guys who's really involved, you know? I'm gonna go to all the baseball games, help with the homework...

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's great, Joe.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I'll teach him to throw a ball, and... and how to talk to girls.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Joey, that's really sweet.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And when he comes home with a girl, I'll just be sitting there cleaning my gun.

jokes.text: Joey says he plans to be in the waiting room handing out cigars when he has a baby
jokes.setup: Someone asks Joey what he'll do when he has a baby, implying he should be more engaged
jokes.punchline: I'm gonna be in the waiting room, handing out cigars.
jokes.explanation: Works well as character comedy — Joey's cheerfully outdated, oblivious machismo is perfectly in character. The joke lands because it's so utterly sincere from him.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh wow, a cigar. You know, that's a really good way to tell the world 'I have no idea what decade I'm living in.'

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Yes, Joey's made arrangements to have his baby in a movie from the '50s.'
jokes.setup: Joey announces his plan to pace in the waiting room and hand out cigars
jokes.punchline: Chandler reframes it as a scene from a 1950s movie, skewering its cultural datedness
jokes.explanation: Sharp Chandler line — economical, specific, and perfectly calibrated. The '50s movie reference is exactly the kind of dry cultural commentary that defines his character. Good economy and structure.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! Eight to the inch!

jokes.text: Phoebe jokes about cab fare structured like contraction pricing: '$2 for the first contraction and 50 cents each additional contraction'
jokes.setup: Ross worries Carol might give birth in the cab
jokes.punchline: Phoebe riffs on cab metered pricing applied to contractions
jokes.explanation: A clever absurdist riff — Phoebe's tangential logic maps taxi meter pricing onto contractions, which is charmingly odd. Not laugh-out-loud but distinctly her flavor of comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why did the chicken cross the road? To get to the other side! No wait, because it was... um... it wanted to prove it wasn't a number!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross, you can't do Chandler. Just stop.

jokes.text: Monica calls out the double standard: 'What, it's okay when Chandler does it?' Reply: 'You have to pick your moments.'
jokes.setup: Monica makes a joke that doesn't land; someone notes Chandler got a laugh for similar humor
jokes.punchline: 'You have to pick your moments' — implying Monica misjudged hers
jokes.explanation: A meta beat that rewards attentive viewers — it calls back Chandler's better joke and gently mocks Monica for trying the same move. Competent but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why did you bring a guitar to the hospital?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, you never know when you're gonna have a spontaneous musical moment. Like, what if someone needs a song? What if the baby comes out and it's all traumatized from being born, and I can soothe it with a little melody?

jokes.text: Ross discovers Carol and Susan stopped at the gift shop — Susan wanted a Chunky
jokes.setup: Ross has been panicking that Carol isn't at the hospital; they finally arrive
jokes.punchline: They stopped at the gift shop for a Chunky candy bar while she was in labor
jokes.explanation: Good comic payoff to the opening tension — the absurdly mundane reason for the delay (a candy bar) perfectly deflates Ross's drama. 'You're having a baby. A baby. You don't stop for Chunkys.' is a solid button.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Where have you been? You're in active labor!

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: We stopped for candy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You stopped for candy? During active labor?

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: They were out of the good kind.

jokes.text: Someone deadpans 'I used to have that bumper sticker' in response to 'You don't stop for Chunkys'
jokes.setup: Ross's outraged declaration that 'you don't stop for Chunkys'
jokes.punchline: Chandler treats it like an actual bumper sticker slogan he's seen before
jokes.explanation: Excellent micro-joke. Maximum economy — four words that reframe Ross's passionate outburst as a trivial piece of pop culture. Pure Chandler deadpan, highly specific. The surprise of it landing in that exact gap is what makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You're telling me that Chandler chose Chunky over Rachel?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Chunky! A candy bar!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: He picked a CANDY BAR over my sister!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What is wrong with him?! What is WRONG with him?!

jokes.text: Carol says each contraction is 'like a little party in my uterus'
jokes.setup: Doctor asks how she's doing with her contractions
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, I love them. Each one's like a little party in my uterus.'
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny line — the cheerful absurdity of 'little party in my uterus' is unexpected, specific, and quotable. Good economy, the image is vivid and ridiculous. One of the episode's stronger one-liners.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's a great bumper sticker.

jokes.text: Ross and Susan fight over who gets to fetch ice chips, both lunging to do it simultaneously
jokes.setup: Doctor says Carol can only have ice chips; Ross and Susan both offer to get them
jokes.punchline: The mundane task of fetching ice chips becomes a proxy battle for dominance between ex-husband and lesbian partner
jokes.explanation: Competent running joke setup — the Ross/Susan rivalry playing out over something trivial is solid character comedy, though the joke itself is fairly predictable in execution.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Franzblau
dialogue.line: I've been thinking of having a baby.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, that's a good start.

jokes.text: They're every four minutes and last 55 seconds. / Fifty-nine seconds. Quartz. / Swiss quartz. Ha, ha.
jokes.setup: Ross provides the precise contraction timing, showing off his obsessive data-tracking.
jokes.punchline: Ross corrects Susan's already precise number, then Dr. Franzblau tops both of them with 'Swiss quartz' — a three-step escalation of absurd precision about something nobody would actually time this carefully.
jokes.explanation: A nicely structured three-beat escalation. The doctor chiming in with 'Swiss quartz' is the unexpected topper — you expect the joke to be Ross vs. Susan, but Franzblau's entry reframes the whole thing as everyone being absurdly competitive about useless precision.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: How are the contractions coming along?

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: Oh, they're great! I'm having a party every five minutes. It's a real blast!

jokes.text: I'll get them [ice chips]. / No, I'm getting it. / No, I got it. I'm getting it.
jokes.setup: Carol asks for ice chips. Ross and Susan both immediately volunteer.
jokes.punchline: The mundane act of fetching ice chips becomes a proxy war between Ross and Susan — even this tiny act of care is something they compete over.
jokes.explanation: A functional character beat that establishes the Ross-Susan rivalry. Not particularly clever writing but effectively shows their dynamic through action rather than exposition.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's not 'it's', it's 'it is'. The contraction is 'it's' with an apostrophe between the 't' and the 's'.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, your arm is falling off!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yes, well, it IS falling off. And look at my Rolex—still keeping perfect time.

jokes.text: Hi. Thought you might like some ice chips. / I... do not believe we have met. Hi.
jokes.setup: Rachel brings ice chips as a pretense to introduce herself to the attractive doctor she noticed.
jokes.punchline: Rachel abandons her ice chip delivery mission mid-sentence when she sees the doctor, pivoting from caregiver to flirt in real time — caught in the act of her own scheme.
jokes.explanation: Rachel's transparent scheme is a solid character beat. The mid-sentence pivot ('I... do not believe we have met') lands because it's so nakedly obvious what she's doing. Competent comedy of character.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I need some ice chips.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Franzblau
dialogue.line: I'll get them for you.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: No, I'll get them for you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's okay, either one of you—

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Franzblau
dialogue.line: I'm getting the ice chips!

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: No, I'm getting them!

jokes.text: Rachel introduces herself as 'Carol's ex-husband's sister's roommate' — doctor mirrors with 'your roommate's brother's ex-wife's obstetrician'
jokes.setup: Rachel gives the convoluted chain of relationships explaining who she is
jokes.punchline: The doctor one-ups her with an equally absurd reverse chain describing himself
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed joke — the mirroring structure is elegant and the payoff earns its laugh. The setup is organic (Rachel genuinely trying to explain herself) and the punchline subverts expectation by the doctor playing along rather than being confused. Good structural craft.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So Ross is my ex, but we have a son together, and now he's married to Emily, who is the sister of my boyfriend Tag, except Tag and I broke up, and now I'm dating Joey, but Joey is also sleeping with Chandler's girlfriend Monica, who is actually married to Chandler, and Ross is also Monica's brother...

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Franzblau
dialogue.line: I see. Well, my wife's sister is married to my wife's brother, who is my wife's other brother's roommate, and my wife's brother is having an affair with my wife's sister's best friend, who is also my therapist's ex-husband's current wife's cousin...

jokes.text: Monica says 'I want a baby' and Phoebe replies 'Not tonight, honey, I got an early day tomorrow'
jokes.setup: Monica, watching the birth preparation, earnestly declares she wants a baby
jokes.punchline: Phoebe responds as if Monica propositioned her for sex, playing the exhausted partner
jokes.explanation: Clean misdirection — Phoebe's response reframes Monica's statement as a romantic proposition, subverting it with a classic deflection line. Economy is high (one short response does all the work). Reliably funny.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I want a baby!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay!

jokes.text: Phoebe suggests getting coffee; Monica says 'Oh, okay, because we never do that' — sarcastically, since coffee is their constant activity
jokes.setup: Phoebe says 'Get up. Come on, let's get some coffee.'
jokes.punchline: Monica's sarcastic 'Oh, okay, because we never do that' — a meta-joke acknowledging the show's coffee-shop trope
jokes.explanation: A rare self-aware moment for Friends — acknowledging the Central Perk coffee obsession meta-textually. Works especially well on rewatch once viewers are fully aware of the show's formula. Slightly underdeveloped but punchy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: We should get coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, because we haven't had coffee in like... four minutes.

jokes.text: Joey tries to argue with a pregnant woman about basketball, then she has a contraction and he panics
jokes.setup: Joey and a stranger (Lydia) get into a heated Knicks vs. Celtics debate
jokes.punchline: She suddenly screams in labor; Joey's machismo instantly evaporates into helpless panic
jokes.explanation: Serviceable situational comedy — Joey's enthusiasm colliding with reality is on-brand. The basketball argument itself is a bit meandering before the payoff arrives.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, hey, hey! Look at that! He's falling down! That's what I call a slam dunk!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Yeah, I'm pretty sure that's not how you're supposed to play basketball, but what do I know?

jokes.text: Shoot, shoot, shoot. / Or just fall down. That's good too.
jokes.setup: Someone (Monica presumably) trips or stumbles as they get up.
jokes.punchline: Chandler's deadpan commentary on the physical mishap — 'Or just fall down. That's good too' — treating a stumble as a valid alternative to the original plan.
jokes.explanation: Sharp Chandler deadpan. The line is efficient — minimal words, maximum dryness. The 'That's good too' framing treats the mishap as a legitimate option, which is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Lydia
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, she couldn't hit the broad side of a barn if she was standing inside it.

jokes.text: Joey tries to insult Celtics: 'They couldn't hit a boat if--' then trails off, realizing he's muddled his own trash talk
jokes.setup: Joey tries to flip Lydia's 'couldn't hit water if standing on a boat' insult back on the Celtics
jokes.punchline: He realizes mid-sentence the metaphor doesn't work in reverse and abandons it: 'Wait.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Joey character moment — his genuine mid-sentence confusion as he realizes the insult doesn't translate is perfectly him. The single word 'Wait.' does tremendous work. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? Well, the Celtics are so bad, they... they make the Knicks look like... wait, no, that doesn't work.

jokes.text: Joey shouts 'We need a father over here!' — Lydia responds 'There's no father'
jokes.setup: Joey panics and tries to find the standard person to summon in an emergency: the father
jokes.punchline: 'There's no father.' — deflates the conventional expectation instantly
jokes.explanation: Clean setup/punchline — Joey's instinct to find 'a father' is immediately undercut. Works efficiently and sets up his unlikely role as Lydia's support.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Where's the father? We need to get the father!

dialogue.speaker: Lydia
dialogue.line: There is no father.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: What do you mean there's no father? There's always a father.

dialogue.speaker: Lydia
dialogue.line: Not in this case.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well... this is awkward.

jokes.text: They suck, all right? / Shut up. You know, it's a rebuilding year.
jokes.setup: Joey and Lydia continue the sports argument after Joey fails to complete his comeback.
jokes.punchline: Joey's blunt 'They suck, all right?' as the conclusion when he can't form an argument, and Lydia's equally defensive 'rebuilding year' excuse — the universal sports fan cope.
jokes.explanation: A functional tag to the sports bit. 'Rebuilding year' is the appropriate sports-fan rationalization and earns recognition from sports-savvy viewers. Joey's blunt concession is in character.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: And then the baby grew up and resented his mother for the choices she made...

jokes.text: 'Thanks, Ross.' / 'Yeah. I'm paying you to stop.'
jokes.setup: Ross finishes his depressing lullaby
jokes.punchline: Carol's flat 'Thanks' followed by immediately offering to pay him to stop
jokes.explanation: Solid button on the lullaby gag — extremely economical. 'I'm paying you to stop' is the perfect deadpan payoff. Slightly conventional in form but well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for that incredibly depressing song.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, you're welcome! Although, I should tell you - people usually have to pay me to stop.

jokes.text: Thanks, Ross. / Yeah. I'm paying you to stop.
jokes.setup: Phoebe finishes her depressing lullaby.
jokes.punchline: Ross thanks her with the weary politeness of someone who just endured something terrible, then reveals he's paying her to stop — meaning he hired her to play and now regrets it.
jokes.explanation: The callback works well. 'I'm paying you to stop' recontextualizes the earlier guitar setup — Ross had a plan, and the plan has catastrophically backfired. Good economy on the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, they're twins? How is that fair? I've been trying to have a baby for years and she just gets two?

jokes.text: Phoebe sees twins and complains 'No fair. I don't even have one. How come they get two?'
jokes.setup: Phoebe spots a couple with newborn twins in the hospital
jokes.punchline: She responds with pure childlike indignation at the perceived injustice of someone getting two babies
jokes.explanation: Charming Phoebe moment — her guileless, unfiltered complaint is very her. The joke is mild but the character specificity keeps it above average.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: And if by some miracle you're not married by the time you're 40, I will marry you.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What do you mean 'if by some miracle'?!

jokes.text: Chandler offers: when we're 40 and neither of us is married, 'what do you say you and I have one?' — Monica immediately spirals
jokes.setup: Chandler makes a casual hypothetical offer to have a baby with Monica when they're 40 if both unmarried
jokes.punchline: Monica latches onto 'if neither of us are married' and interprets it as Chandler implying she's fundamentally unmarriable
jokes.explanation: Strong character comedy setup — Chandler's foot-in-mouth hypothetical is entirely believable, and Monica's immediate over-interpretation plays well on rewatch knowing their eventual relationship. Her escalating spiral ('Is there something fundamentally unmarriable about me?') is well-structured.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So when are you getting married?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Monica, we've talked about this.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I know, but I'm ready now. Aren't you?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yes, eventually.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Eventually? What does that mean? A year? Two years?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't know, Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You know what? You're fundamentally unmarriable. That's just who you are as a person.

jokes.text: Chandler, trapped by Monica's questioning, panics and blurts 'Dear God. This parachute is a knapsack.'
jokes.setup: Monica is pressing Chandler to answer whether there's something 'fundamentally unmarriable' about her; he is cornered
jokes.punchline: Chandler randomly invokes a parachute/knapsack metaphor to fake an emergency and escape the conversation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and arguably one of the best Chandler moments of Season 1. The line is perfectly absurd — specific enough to be funny ('knapsack' not 'backpack'), escalates the desperation naturally, and is delivered as pure panic. It captures Chandler's pathological avoidance of emotional directness. Highly quotable, exceptional economy. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in quality — this one edges past it due to originality and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm like a guy on a sinking ship who keeps rearranging the deck chairs. Monica's great, but nobody's buying tickets.

jokes.text: 'Rachel, what is the deal with you and doctors? Is, like, your father a doctor?' / 'Yeah. Why?' / 'No reason.'
jokes.setup: Monica notices Rachel's obsession with Dr. Franzblau and implies a Freudian explanation
jokes.punchline: 'No reason.' — Monica drops the Freudian inference without spelling it out, letting the implication land
jokes.explanation: Smart, economical joke — the 'No reason' does all the heavy lifting. Monica implies a daddy-issues Freudian analysis without ever saying it, trusting the audience to make the connection. Very well-structured for a three-line exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why are you so interested in doctors?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I don't know what you're talking about.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Come on, you've been asking about every doctor you meet.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So?

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So... you like doctors!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, fine. I like doctors. Is that so bad?

jokes.text: Lydia's mother calls; Lydia says she's not alone — 'Joey's here' — then mouths 'Joey who?' to Joey
jokes.setup: Lydia is on the phone with her mother, saying she's not alone
jokes.punchline: She proudly names 'Joey' and then immediately turns to mouth 'Joey who?' — she doesn't even know his last name
jokes.explanation: Sweet and funny — the physical mouthing of 'Joey who?' is a good visual beat that plays well. The self-correction in real-time while on a phone call is a reliable comedic device executed cleanly.

dialogue.speaker: Lydia's Mother
dialogue.line: Who is this?

dialogue.speaker: Lydia
dialogue.line: Mom, this is Joey.

dialogue.speaker: Lydia's Mother
dialogue.line: Joey who?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Joey Tribbiani. We've met like... five times.

jokes.text: Joey talks to Lydia's mother on the phone; she hangs up when he says he's an actor
jokes.setup: Lydia's mom wants to talk to Joey; he cheerfully gives his stats (age, single, actor)
jokes.punchline: The line goes dead the moment he says 'actor' — the universal maternal red flag
jokes.explanation: Predictable but well-executed — the beat where the phone goes silent after 'An actor' is a classic joke that works because of Joey's complete obliviousness to why it happened.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wow, she hung up on you. That's a little rude.

jokes.text: She wants to talk to you. / No. / Take the phone. / Hi. Yeah, it's me. / Oh, no, no, no. We're just friends. Yeah. / Yeah, I'm single. / Twenty-five. / An actor. / Hello?
jokes.setup: Joey is forced to talk to Lydia's skeptical mother on the phone.
jokes.punchline: Joey immediately abandons any pretense of reassurance and starts hitting on the mother (or at least fully auditioning for her approval as a romantic prospect), ending with her hanging up.
jokes.explanation: A great Joey moment. The escalating self-introduction (name, age, job) turning into a dating pitch during an inappropriate phone call is pure Joey. The mother hanging up is the perfect punctuation. The 'Hello?' at the end — delivered into dead air — is the cherry on top.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You know, having a kid, it's gonna change your life. But in a good way. You're gonna have someone to love unconditionally.

dialogue.speaker: Lydia
dialogue.line: That's nice, but I didn't ask for your advice.

jokes.text: Ross and Susan argue about the baby's name — Jordy vs. Jamie, with Susan's first girlfriend backstory and the 'Jesse/Cody/Dillon fiasco'
jokes.setup: They try to calm Carol by focusing on the baby's name 'Jordy'
jokes.punchline: Ross objects to Jordy; it emerges the name went through a ridiculous journey: Jesse/Cody/Dillon were all rejected before, and Susan's first girlfriend ruins 'Jamie'
jokes.explanation: Strong escalating joke — each revelation builds on the last. 'The whole Jesse/Cody/Dillon fiasco' is an excellently throwaway reference to implied prior drama. Good ensemble character comedy revealing everyone's petty stakes.

dialogue.speaker: Roy
dialogue.line: Is this Lydia?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, this is Joey. But you can rent me by the hour.

jokes.text: Carol gets a leg cramp; Ross and Susan fight over who gets to massage it — 'You get to sleep with her. I get the cramps.'
jokes.setup: Carol screams from a leg cramp; both Ross and Susan lunge to help
jokes.punchline: Susan delivers the line 'You get to sleep with her. I get the cramps.' — asserting her right via intimacy
jokes.explanation: Sharp line that encapsulates the whole Ross/Susan dynamic — Susan claiming the right to help Carol via their intimacy, implicitly reminding Ross of his displacement. Works on character and situational levels simultaneously.

jokes.text: That is it. I want both of you out. / She started it. / He started it.
jokes.setup: Carol kicks Ross and Susan out of the delivery room after their constant bickering.
jokes.punchline: Both adults immediately respond with the most childish possible defense — 'She/He started it' — in the room where Carol is literally giving birth to an actual child.
jokes.explanation: 'She started it / He started it' is an overused device — but the context (adults being childish in a literal delivery room) gives it enough situational irony to work. The writing is lazy but the situation redeems it somewhat.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So who won?

dialogue.speaker: Lydia
dialogue.line: My team did! You know, I have to say, I was wrong about those guys earlier. They're actually pretty good.

jokes.text: Carol kicks both Ross and Susan out of the delivery room mid-argument: 'I'm trying to get a person out of my body here'
jokes.setup: Ross and Susan continue bickering during Carol's labor
jokes.punchline: Carol's brutally matter-of-fact delivery: 'I'm trying to get a person out of my body here, and you're not making it any easier. Now go!'
jokes.explanation: Well-earned payoff — Carol's patience finally snapping is satisfying after watching the squabbling. 'Getting a person out of my body' is a memorably vivid phrase that grounds the absurdity in biology.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. You changed it? To Jordy? But we agreed on Emma!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I know, but I was thinking—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You were thinking? We had a spreadsheet, Rachel. A COLOR-CODED spreadsheet. With footnotes. I have three backup copies in a safe deposit box.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's just a name—

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Just a name?! Do you remember the negotiation process? Seventeen meetings. I created a PowerPoint presentation. We eliminated Jordan because it's unisex, we ruled out Jordy because it's 'too casual,' and now... now you're telling me you picked Jordy?

jokes.text: Hospital staff react with 'Ew' and 'Something exploded' when Carol's water breaks
jokes.setup: Carol's water breaks in the delivery room
jokes.punchline: The friends in the hallway react with visceral disgust — 'What is that? Something exploded'
jokes.explanation: Functional gross-out reaction beat — the friends' horrified response is relatable but the joke doesn't have strong craft. Works on audience recognition level but isn't cleverly constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: She gets the massage, I get the nausea.

jokes.text: What is that? Something exploded. / It's just her water breaking. Calm down, will you?
jokes.setup: Lydia's water breaks in the room Joey has followed her into.
jokes.punchline: Joey's alarmed 'Something exploded' treats a normal part of labor like a catastrophic mechanical failure — his ignorance of basic biology is the joke.
jokes.explanation: 'Something exploded' is a funny framing — Joey's complete lack of medical knowledge presented as a genuine emergency assessment. Lydia's flat dismissal sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: I'm going to push the baby out now.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: That's it? That's all you have to say?

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: What do you want me to say? I'm having a baby. It's coming out.

jokes.text: Ross blames Susan for Carol throwing them out: 'Carol never threw me out of a room before you came along.' Susan: 'Well, there's a lot of things Carol never did before I came along.'
jokes.setup: Ross blames Susan for being ejected
jokes.punchline: Susan's retort implies she's responsible for Carol's entire sexual and personal awakening, including leaving Ross
jokes.explanation: Excellent line — Susan's comeback is devastating, implied rather than stated, and cuts to the core of Ross's deepest insecurity. The economy is superb; 'there's a lot of things Carol never did before I came along' carries enormous weight. Gets a genuine laugh with an edge to it.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God! The water just broke! We're gonna explode!

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Ross, that's not what that means.

jokes.text: Phoebe intervenes in Ross and Susan's fight with an impassioned speech, then shouts 'Don't make me do this again! I don't like my voice like this!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe mediates between Ross and Susan with a serious moral argument
jokes.punchline: She breaks the serious tone by complaining she doesn't like how she sounds when she shouts — a completely self-focused exit from her own earnest lecture
jokes.explanation: Very Phoebe — she deflates her own serious moment with a self-absorbed non sequitur about her own voice. The tonal whiplash is effective and the line has strong character integration. Gets a big laugh from the unexpected pivot.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: This is all your fault!

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: My fault? Maybe if you'd been a better boyfriend, Carol wouldn't have needed to leave you for a woman.

jokes.text: Ross, Phoebe, and Susan are trapped in a hospital room and shout for help
jokes.setup: The trio accidentally locks themselves in a room while Carol is in labor without them
jokes.punchline: All three desperately shouting 'Help!' while Ross tries various futile escape attempts
jokes.explanation: Broad farce setup — getting locked away from the birth is a classic comedic device. Functional but not clever; the joke is entirely in execution rather than writing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You guys, you guys! Stop fighting. Do you know what the babies' first impression of the world is gonna be? Fighting noises!

jokes.text: 'What are you gonna do, suck the door open?'
jokes.setup: Ross is pressing his face or hands against a closed door trying futile escape methods
jokes.punchline: Susan's contemptuous one-liner mocking his useless effort
jokes.explanation: Strong single line — 'suck the door open' is a vivid, specific, contemptuous image. High economy. Susan's disdain for Ross perfectly channeled in one image.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Ross, Susan, you need to listen to me. I'm very disappointed in both of you.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Why do I sound like my mother right now? This is freaking me out.

jokes.text: Phoebe, trapped in the room, sings an increasingly dark song: 'And they found their bodies the very next day'
jokes.setup: The trio is stuck in the room; Phoebe starts singing to cope
jokes.punchline: Her song immediately turns to dark mortality — 'they found their bodies the very next day' — then she catches herself and switches to 'La la la'
jokes.explanation: Superb Phoebe moment — her default to a cheerful folk song that immediately becomes a murder ballad is deeply in character and unexpected. The self-correction to 'La la la' is perfect. Strong character integration, dark humor that still feels like Phoebe. One of her best moments this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's gonna work. Just keep banging on it like that.

jokes.text: Monica on the phone to their mom about Ross: 'He's in a whole other place. Yeah. No, he's gone.' — while we know he's literally stuck in a room
jokes.setup: Mom asks Monica if Ross is okay; Monica reassures her
jokes.punchline: Her metaphorical 'he's in a whole other place, he's gone' is literally true — he's locked in a different room
jokes.explanation: Enjoyable dramatic irony — the audience gets double meaning from 'he's gone' that Monica doesn't intend. Not flashy but effective situational comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Ross is doing great!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Well, okay, he's doing fine.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Actually, he's okay.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's... he's gone.

jokes.text: Monica tells her mom 'I'm not even thinking about babies yet' while hearing a baby coo, then immediately bursts into tears
jokes.setup: Monica insists to her mother she's not thinking about babies at all
jokes.punchline: The instant sound of a baby cooing reduces her to sobbing tears; Chandler mimics static to cover for her
jokes.explanation: Well-constructed irony — the immediate contradiction between her denial and her tearful reaction is perfectly timed. Chandler's static mimicry is a lovely small grace note. Strong emotional and comedic payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: I don't want babies. I'm not interested in having kids.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: *hears baby cooing sounds* Oh my God... *immediately tears up* I need a baby so badly!

jokes.text: [Chandler does a static-crackling noise into the phone to pretend the call is cutting out as Monica cries]
jokes.setup: Monica is breaking down on the phone with her mother after being emotionally overwhelmed by the baby.
jokes.punchline: Chandler, rather than comfort her, fakes static crackle to help her end the call — a hilariously practical but emotionally avoidant move.
jokes.explanation: A lovely Chandler moment — his response to an emotional situation is a practical, slightly cowardly workaround. The static-crackle is a physical comedy beat that perfectly encapsulates Chandler's discomfort with genuine emotion. Character-specific and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Where have you been? I haven't seen you in days!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, yeah, I got married.

jokes.text: Joey returns and announces 'I just had a baby.' / 'Mazel tov.'
jokes.setup: The group asks where Joey has been
jokes.punchline: 'I just had a baby' — Joey has fully taken ownership of Lydia's birth experience; Chandler's deadpan 'Mazel tov' accepts this completely
jokes.explanation: Wonderful economy — two lines do enormous work. Joey's complete appropriation of the birth experience and Chandler's utterly unfazed acceptance of it is perfectly observed. 'Mazel tov' as a one-word punchline is elegantly chosen. High character integration, extremely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Franzblau
dialogue.line: I have trouble dating.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh please, you're a doctor. Women love that.

jokes.text: Dr. Franzblau tries to explain why dating is hard for OB/GYNs, trails off awkwardly: '...where I do' / '...what I do'
jokes.setup: Dr. Franzblau says it's hard to get women to go out with him; Rachel says she's heard it's easy for cute doctors
jokes.punchline: He explains it's because of where he works — trailing off into implication — then compares her coffee shop complaints to his workplace context
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe comedy — the repeated euphemistic trailing off about his work ('where I do... what I do') creates uncomfortable and funny tension. The coffee shop comparison is a neat structural parallel.

dialogue.speaker: Doctor
dialogue.line: You know, my work is like a cup of coffee. It's hot, it's bitter, and it keeps me up all night.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: That's... that's a really great analogy.

jokes.text: It's hard enough to get women to go out with me. / Heh. Right, yeah, I've heard that about cute doctors.
jokes.setup: Franzblau is self-deprecatingly claiming women don't want to date him.
jokes.punchline: Rachel's 'I've heard that about cute doctors' — calling him cute while pretending it's a commonly known fact — a blatant but charming flirting move.
jokes.explanation: Standard flirtatious banter. The 'I've heard that about cute doctors' line is a competent flirt but not particularly clever writing. Works for character establishment but isn't a strong joke on its own.

dialogue.speaker: Roy
dialogue.line: Is this the woman having your baby?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: No, no, no. It's a loaner.

jokes.text: 'If I see one more cup of coffee' — Rachel takes a beat, then agrees she gets it
jokes.setup: Dr. Franzblau compares his OB/GYN professional fatigue to a waitress being sick of coffee
jokes.punchline: Rachel's dawning understanding that seeing 'one more cup of coffee' is nothing compared to what he sees — and her diplomatic agreement
jokes.explanation: Good button on the flirtation scene — the awkward moment of Rachel realizing the asymmetry of their complaints is well-executed. The comedy is more of a reaction beat than a punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: I feel like no one in your family acknowledges me or my relationship with Carol.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? We celebrate your relationship every day.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's called Lesbian Visibility Day.

jokes.text: Lydia says she wasn't alone during birth — 'I had a doctor, a nurse and a helper guy' — referring to Joey
jokes.setup: Roy expresses regret that Lydia was alone
jokes.punchline: She lists 'a doctor, a nurse and a helper guy' — the absurdly vague description of Joey's role reduces him to generic support personnel
jokes.explanation: 'Helper guy' as Joey's official title is endearingly funny — the casual diminishment of his participation. Good economy, the joke is in the specificity of the vague.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about my whole family situation, and I realize it's not so bad. I mean, sure, my mom had me with my stepfather, and then she married my biological father, and then... okay, it's confusing. But you know what? I have so much love in my life. Some people don't have any parents, and I have like... four. That's abundance!

jokes.text: Lydia and Roy's relationship reversal: after the game, Lydia says 'Knicks by 10, they suck' — Roy says 'Eh, they're not so bad'
jokes.setup: Earlier, Lydia was vocally anti-Knicks; Roy is now the absent father she's been dismissive of
jokes.punchline: She now casually trashes the Knicks while Roy defends them — their positions have swapped, undercutting her earlier posturing
jokes.explanation: Neat structural callback — her earlier passionate anti-Knicks stance now reversed creates a light irony that pays off the subplot. Not big laughs but satisfying storytelling.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I can't find the, uh... the thing that goes... *makes vague gesturing motions* ...you know, the medical part.

jokes.text: Ross: 'When this day is over, you get to go home with the baby.' / Susan: 'Where does that leave me?' / Ross: 'You get to be the father.' / Susan: 'There's no Lesbian Lover Day.' / Ross: 'Every day is Lesbian Lover Day.'
jokes.setup: Ross and Susan have a genuine moment of vulnerability in the locked room — each expressing their fear of being left out
jokes.punchline: Susan complains there's no 'Lesbian Lover Day'; Ross fires back 'Every day is Lesbian Lover Day' — his best zinger of the episode
jokes.explanation: The episode's standout joke. The exchange escalates into Ross's comeback 'Every day is Lesbian Lover Day' — perfectly timed, deeply character-specific, and genuinely clever. It has the structure of a great sitcom retort: it sounds like a non-answer but contains real wit. The specificity ('Lesbian Lover Day') is both funny as a concept and serves the character conflict. Highly quotable, great economy. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor — this surpasses it slightly on character integration and originality.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Hi, I'm Ben. Ben Parker. I work here at the hospital.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But by night, I fight crime as... Spider-Man!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, that's not right either.

jokes.text: There's Father's Day. There's Mother's Day. There's no Lesbian Lover Day. / Every day is Lesbian Lover Day.
jokes.setup: Susan complains about the lack of recognition for her role as Carol's partner — there's no holiday for her.
jokes.punchline: Ross's comeback — 'Every day is Lesbian Lover Day' — is meant as a dismissal but is hilariously presented as though he's genuinely conceding the point, or perhaps enviously observing that Susan has it good.
jokes.explanation: A strong exchange. 'Every day is Lesbian Lover Day' is Ross's attempt at a put-down that accidentally sounds like he's conceding her point, or even expressing wistfulness. The quotability is high — it's the kind of line that sounds like a genuine non-sequitur comeback but has internal logic. Well-constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh! Oh my God! There's a dead bird in there!

jokes.text: 'Uh-- Oh, that's great. Anybody seen a nipple?'
jokes.setup: The birth is happening chaotically with everyone crowding the room
jokes.punchline: Dr. Franzblau, in full professional mode, casually asks if anyone has seen a nipple — presumably for a breast pump or feeding preparation, but the context makes it maximally awkward
jokes.explanation: Good cringe-discomfort joke — the doctor's completely blasé professional question lands as hilariously inappropriate in the crowded room. Economy is high; the line works on pure unexpected context.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh my God, is he okay? He's stuck half in, half out!

jokes.text: Phoebe reports from inside the vent: 'Well, Susan, I see what appears to be a dark vent. Wait. Yes, it is, in fact, a dark vent.'
jokes.setup: Susan asks what Phoebe can see through the vent opening
jokes.punchline: Phoebe does a mock-serious reporter build-up only to confirm: it's a dark vent
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist deadpan — Phoebe's build-up with 'what appears to be' followed by the utterly obvious conclusion ('a dark vent') is a perfect comedic anticlimax. Well-structured and distinctly Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Franzblau
dialogue.line: Okay people, I need everyone except the father out of the delivery room.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That would be me.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Franzblau
dialogue.line: Actually, I'm going to need you to wait outside too. You're making me very uncomfortable.

jokes.text: 'Wait! You forgot your legs!' — as Ross climbs through the vent
jokes.setup: Ross is escaping through the vent headfirst
jokes.punchline: Phoebe shouts 'You forgot your legs!' — a literally meaningless warning delivered with complete urgency
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly absurd Phoebe line — 'you forgot your legs' makes zero logical sense (legs don't get 'forgotten') but lands perfectly as panicked, well-intentioned nonsense. Five words, maximum comedy. Pure character, high economy. One of the episode's best single-line jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So the doctor said I can't have caffeine anymore.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: But there's an exemption for people with my condition.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So I asked him, 'Do I qualify?' And he said, 'No, you're just nervous.'

jokes.text: Dr. Franzblau: 'There's too many people in this room. There's about to be one more. So anybody who's not an ex-husband or a lesbian life partner, out you go.'
jokes.setup: The room is crowded with all the friends; the birth is imminent
jokes.punchline: The doctor's absurdly specific list of who gets to stay — 'ex-husband or lesbian life partner' — casually normalizing the unusual family structure
jokes.explanation: Smart joke — the doctor's unfazed professional recitation of 'ex-husband or lesbian life partner' as standard delivery room criteria is both funny and progressively warm. The casualness of acceptance is the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Oh my God. That's not coming out of there!

jokes.text: Joey asks the nurse: 'Let me ask you, do you have to be Carol's lesbian life partner?'
jokes.setup: The doctor kicks non-essential people out; Joey tries to find a loophole to stay
jokes.punchline: Joey's attempt to claim the 'lesbian life partner' designation — completely earnest, completely oblivious
jokes.explanation: Excellent Joey moment — his guileless attempt to claim the 'lesbian life partner' slot to stay in the room is perfectly in character. The earnestness makes it funnier than any knowingly clever version of this joke would be.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What does he look like?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, he's got Monica's eyes, and my nose, and he's got this weird, angry expression on his face...

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Aww!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, he looks like an old man. Like an angry old man who's mad that we woke him up.

jokes.text: Ross watches the birth: 'Oh. It's huge. Carol, how are you doing this?' / 'Not helping.'
jokes.setup: Ross watches the baby crowning and is overwhelmed
jokes.punchline: 'It's huge. Carol, how are you doing this?' gets the flat response 'Not helping.'
jokes.explanation: Reliable joke form — the oblivious comment met with the deadpan 'not helping' retort. The setup is perhaps predictable but 'It's huge, Carol, how are you doing this?' is specifically Ross, and Carol's response is perfectly timed.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We made it up.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You made up the name?

dialogue.speaker: Carol
dialogue.line: We were trapped in the cabin during the storm.

dialogue.speaker: Susan
dialogue.line: We needed a story, so we invented the whole thing.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, we just made up a name to cover for being stuck there.

jokes.text: Ross describes the newborn baby as looking 'kind of like my Uncle Ed, covered in Jell-O'
jokes.setup: Friends ask what the baby looks like
jokes.punchline: 'Kind of like my Uncle Ed, covered in Jell-O.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The unexpected specificity of 'Uncle Ed' combined with 'covered in Jell-O' is perfectly calibrated — specific enough to be real, absurd enough to be funny, and instantly visual. The Jell-O comparison for amniotic fluid is inspired. Highly quotable, strong economy, original image. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and arguably funnier due to specificity.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, he looks just like you!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: No, not at all.

jokes.text: Phoebe shouts congratulations on the baby from above — in the vent
jokes.setup: Everyone celebrates the birth; Phoebe is still in the vent
jokes.punchline: 'Phoebe [FROM ABOVE]: You guys, he's beautiful.' — she's still stuck watching from the ventilation shaft
jokes.explanation: Sweet visual callback — Phoebe's perspective from inside the vent is a charming payoff to the B-plot. The emotion of the moment isn't undercut but the absurdity of where she is amplifies it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, I still act like a baby and I don't have one of those things!

jokes.text: The baby is named Ben — inspired by 'Hospital Worker Ben' from the vent rescue
jokes.setup: The doctor notes they still need a name for the baby
jokes.punchline: Someone suggests 'Ben' — and it's adopted, with the implication it came from the random janitor who rescued them from the vent
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback payoff — the baby's name comes from the vent rescue janitor, which is both absurd and structurally satisfying. The parents' cover story ('we just cooked it up') is a nice wink. One of the episode's best structural comedy moments.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Hi! I'm Aunt Monica. And I'm gonna be the cool aunt who always has gum.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: You're gonna love me.

jokes.text: Susan: 'He looks just like you.' — said to Ross about the baby
jokes.setup: Everyone is admiring the newborn Ben
jokes.punchline: Susan — Carol's lesbian partner who has been Ross's rival all episode — tells Ross the baby looks just like him, in a moment of genuine warmth that's also funny coming from her
jokes.explanation: Sweet character beat — Susan's warmth toward Ross in this moment lands as genuinely funny given their dynamic all episode. Not a huge laugh but a satisfying character comedy moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Hey buddy, Daddy's here now. Daddy's always here for you.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, except Tuesdays and Thursdays when I coach little league.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: And the occasional weekend when there's a really important dinosaur thing.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: But other than that, Daddy's here.

jokes.text: 'I can't believe one of us actually has one of these.' / 'I know. I still am one of these.'
jokes.setup: Friends marvel at the new baby
jokes.punchline: Chandler's deflection: 'I still am one of these' — claiming emotional immaturity / childlikeness
jokes.explanation: Perfect Chandler line — maximum economy, self-deprecating, character-specific. His admission of being emotionally a baby himself is both funny and true to his character. One of his better one-liners of the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Hey, Jack! Jack! Come on, buddy, look at me. Jack!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: He's three months old.

jokes.text: Monica holds Ben, addresses him formally: 'I'm your Aunt Monica. Yes, I am. I will always have gum.'
jokes.setup: Monica holds the baby and begins introducing herself
jokes.punchline: Her solemn promise to the newborn: 'I will always have gum' — as if this is her most important quality as an aunt
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The comedic bathos of promising a newborn 'I will always have gum' as a solemn vow is perfectly unexpected and specific. It's the kind of joke that only works because of the gravity of the setup — Monica holding the baby, the emotional music, and then: gum. Strong economy, originality, and earned comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So what does the baby do?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, right now he sleeps most of the time.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, that's great! So it's like living with Monica!

jokes.text: Ross does a series of 'peek-a-boo' style approaches and retreats with Ben, explaining he might sometimes be away
jokes.setup: Ross promises Ben he'll always come back, even when away
jokes.punchline: He physically demonstrates this by repeatedly appearing and disappearing from Ben's view — including a baseball steal-third signal 'like this'
jokes.explanation: Charming physical bit — Ross's overly literal demonstration of 'coming back' is sweet and funny. The escalating absurdity of the baseball signal is a fun non sequitur. More visual than verbal, plays better on screen.

jokes.text: Chandler calls Ben by name to test it; gets no reaction; declares 'Nothing. I don't think that's his name.'
jokes.setup: Everyone is gathered around baby Ben; Chandler tries calling his name
jokes.punchline: 'Nothing. I don't think that's his name.' — as if a newborn should be responding to roll call
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chandler joke — his deadpan logic that the baby not responding proves his name is wrong is absurd yet perfectly in character. 'Nothing. I don't think that's his name.' has strong economy and character integration. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Friends comment on the baby in real-time: 'Oh, look, look, he's closing his eyes.' / 'Oh, look, he's opening his eyes.' / 'He doesn't do much, does he?' / 'Nope, this is pretty much it.'
jokes.setup: The friends gather around the newborn, watching him intently
jokes.punchline: After narrating his every micro-movement, someone delivers the deflating verdict: 'He doesn't do much, does he?' / 'Nope, this is pretty much it.'
jokes.explanation: Solid observational bit — the gap between the reverence with which the friends treat every micro-expression and the honest assessment ('he doesn't do much') is a reliable comedic form executed well. The structure builds nicely.

jokes.text: Joey blows a raspberry at the baby; Chandler mirrors it; they marvel as Ben closes his eyes again
jokes.setup: The emotional closing scene of friends with the newborn
jokes.punchline: Joey blows a raspberry; Chandler immediately does the same — two grown men defaulting to the most basic baby interaction possible
jokes.explanation: Warm closing physical beat — Joey and Chandler's synchronized raspberry is a sweet, funny image that ends the episode on a light note. More charming than clever, but fits the tone perfectly.

tmdb_overview: As Monica's biological clock ticks away like a time bomb, Carol goes into labor. Ross, Susan and Phoebe end up getting locked in a closet just as Carol's about to give birth to the baby. And Rachel flirts with an OB/GYN.
insight: Season finale trades jokes for heart: 70-point humor index masks emotional weight over laughs.
